episode.title: The Moon That Leaks an Ocean
episode.central_question: Is something alive in the ocean under the ice of Enceladus?

beats.name: A moon that should be dead
beats.because: But a moon that small should be frozen solid.

beats.name: The discovery
beats.because: Therefore only a closer look could explain it.

beats.name: The hidden ocean
beats.because: But where was all that water coming from?

beats.name: The ingredients
beats.because: Therefore the next question: could it support life?

beats.name: Life without sunlight
beats.because: Therefore we look at Earth, where that chemistry already feeds life.

beats.name: What we still don't know
beats.because: But Cassini could not answer the last question.

beats.name: The answer
beats.because: Therefore the answer is still open.

shots.voiceover: In 2005, a spacecraft circling Saturn noticed something odd about one of its smallest moons.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: In 2005, a spacecraft circling Saturn noticed something odd about one of its smallest moons.

shots.voiceover: Something there was pushing back against Saturn's magnetic field.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: Something there was pushing back against Saturn's magnetic field.

shots.voiceover: Months later, Cassini flew in for a closer look.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: And it saw this: water, spraying out of a frozen moon, into space.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: This is the real image.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

shots.voiceover: A moon barely five hundred kilometres across, leaking an ocean.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: A moon barely five hundred kilometres across, leaking an ocean.

shots.voiceover: Today we follow that water down, to the ocean it came from.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: And we ask the question scientists now ask out loud: could something be alive down there?

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Enceladus is one of Saturn's smaller moons.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Small worlds lose their heat fast. They freeze solid, and they stay that way.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: When Voyager 2 flew past in 1981, it saw something that didn't fit.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL

claims.text: When Voyager 2 flew past in 1981, it saw something that didn't fit.

shots.voiceover: Whole regions were smooth, with no craters at all. Something had been repaving this moon.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: Whole regions were smooth, with no craters at all. Something had been repaving this moon.

shots.voiceover: Fresh ice. Long fractures. A surface that looked young.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

shots.voiceover: Voyager only had a glimpse. The answer had to wait more than twenty years.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Cassini reached Saturn in 2004.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: Cassini reached Saturn in 2004.

shots.voiceover: In February 2005, its magnetometer felt Saturn's magnetic field bending around Enceladus, as if something like an atmosphere was in the way.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: In February 2005, its magnetometer felt Saturn's magnetic field bending around Enceladus, as if something like an atmosphere was in the way.

shots.voiceover: In July, Cassini found a cloud of water vapour hanging over the south pole.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: In July, Cassini found a cloud of water vapour hanging over the south pole.

shots.voiceover: Below it were four long, warm fractures in the ice. Scientists called them tiger stripes.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: Below it were four long, warm fractures in the ice. Scientists called them tiger stripes.

shots.voiceover: Each one is about a hundred and thirty-five kilometres long.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: Each one is about a hundred and thirty-five kilometres long.

shots.voiceover: Over the years, Cassini counted a hundred and one separate geysers along them.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: Over the years, Cassini counted a hundred and one separate geysers along them.

shots.voiceover: And the south pole was not just warm for an ice moon. It was hot.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: It gives off about sixteen gigawatts of heat, around two and a half times the power of all the hot springs in Yellowstone.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/GSFC/SwRI/SSI

claims.text: It gives off about sixteen gigawatts of heat, around two and a half times the power of all the hot springs in Yellowstone.

shots.voiceover: The spray was not a thin mist. It was feeding an entire ring of Saturn.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/SSI

claims.text: The spray was not a thin mist. It was feeding an entire ring of Saturn.

shots.voiceover: Saturn's faint outer E ring is made mostly of ice from these jets.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: Saturn's faint outer E ring is made mostly of ice from these jets.

shots.voiceover: So where was all that water coming from?

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Ice can turn straight into vapour without ever melting. Scientists needed proof of liquid water.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: The proof was salt.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: In 2009, Cassini found sodium salts in ice grains from Saturn's outer ring, the ring Enceladus feeds.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: In 2009, Cassini found sodium salts in ice grains from Saturn's outer ring, the ring Enceladus feeds.

shots.voiceover: Salt like that dissolves out of rock, in liquid water. Somewhere below, water was touching stone.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: By 2014, gravity measurements pointed to a sea under the south pole, about ten kilometres deep, under thirty to forty kilometres of ice.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

claims.text: By 2014, gravity measurements pointed to a sea under the south pole, about ten kilometres deep, under thirty to forty kilometres of ice.

shots.voiceover: Then came a stranger clue. Enceladus wobbles as it orbits Saturn.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Scientists tracked craters across hundreds of Cassini images, taken over more than seven years.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: Scientists tracked craters across hundreds of Cassini images, taken over more than seven years.

shots.voiceover: The wobble was too large for a moon frozen solid. The ice shell had to be floating.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: The wobble was too large for a moon frozen solid. The ice shell had to be floating.

shots.voiceover: In 2015 came the verdict: a global ocean, wrapped around the entire moon.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

claims.text: In 2015 came the verdict: a global ocean, wrapped around the entire moon.

shots.voiceover: A hidden ocean, on a moon with roughly the surface area of Turkey.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

shots.voiceover: Life as we know it needs three things: liquid water, a source of energy, and the right chemistry.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Water, Enceladus clearly has.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: In 2008, Cassini flew straight through the plume and tasted it.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute

claims.text: In 2008, Cassini flew straight through the plume and tasted it.

shots.voiceover: It was full of organic molecules, about twenty times denser than expected.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: It was full of organic molecules, about twenty times denser than expected.

shots.voiceover: Scientists compared it to carbonated water with an essence of natural gas.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: Scientists compared it to carbonated water with an essence of natural gas.

shots.voiceover: In 2015, tiny grains of silica pointed to something more: hot water reacting with rock, on the ocean floor.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

claims.text: In 2015, tiny grains of silica pointed to something more: hot water reacting with rock, on the ocean floor.

shots.voiceover: Then, on the 28th of October 2015, Cassini made its deepest dive through the plume.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: Then, on the 28th of October 2015, Cassini made its deepest dive through the plume.

shots.voiceover: It found hydrogen, about one percent of the gas.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: It found hydrogen, about one percent of the gas.

shots.voiceover: Hydrogen like that forms when hot water reacts with rock. And for microbes, it is food: chemical energy.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

claims.text: Hydrogen like that forms when hot water reacts with rock. And for microbes, it is food: chemical energy.

shots.voiceover: In 2023, one more ingredient: phosphates, at least a hundred times more concentrated than in Earth's oceans.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

claims.text: In 2023, one more ingredient: phosphates, at least a hundred times more concentrated than in Earth's oceans.

shots.voiceover: Phosphorus forms the backbone of every DNA molecule on Earth.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: Phosphorus forms the backbone of every DNA molecule on Earth.

shots.voiceover: Water. Energy. Chemistry. Every box we know how to tick.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: To see what that chemistry can do, we only have to look at home.

visual.credit: NASA (JSC)

shots.voiceover: Two and a half kilometres below the Pacific, there is no sunlight at all.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Solar System Scope Earth map (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data)

claims.text: Two and a half kilometres below the Pacific, there is no sunlight at all.

shots.voiceover: In 1977, scientists exploring the Galápagos Rift found hot springs on the seafloor, and life crowded around them.

visual.credit: NOAA Office of Ocean Exploration and Research
visual.credit_short: NOAA Office of Ocean Exploration and Research

claims.text: In 1977, scientists exploring the Galápagos Rift found hot springs on the seafloor, and life crowded around them.

shots.voiceover: Clams, crabs, tubeworms, living in total darkness.

visual.credit: OAR/National Undersea Research Program (NURP)

claims.text: Clams, crabs, tubeworms, living in total darkness.

shots.voiceover: At the base of that food web are microbes that live on chemistry, not sunlight.

visual.credit: IFE, URI-IAO, UW, Lost City Science Party; NOAA/OAR/OER; The Lost City 2005 Expedition
visual.credit_short: IFE, URI-IAO, UW, Lost City Science Party

claims.text: At the base of that food web are microbes that live on chemistry, not sunlight.

shots.voiceover: At places like the Lost City vent field in the Atlantic, hydrogen from the rocks feeds them.

visual.credit: IFE, URI-IAO, UW, Lost City Science Party; NOAA/OAR/OER; The Lost City 2005 Expedition
visual.credit_short: IFE, URI-IAO, UW, Lost City Science Party

claims.text: At places like the Lost City vent field in the Atlantic, hydrogen from the rocks feeds them.

shots.voiceover: Hydrogen. Carbon dioxide. Warm rock. Liquid water. The same recipe Cassini found at Enceladus.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: Hydrogen. Carbon dioxide. Warm rock. Liquid water. The same recipe Cassini found at Enceladus.

shots.voiceover: Some scientists think life on Earth itself may have started at vents like these.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Cassini was built before anyone knew Enceladus had an ocean. It could not detect life.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

claims.text: Cassini was built before anyone knew Enceladus had an ocean. It could not detect life.

shots.voiceover: On the 15th of September 2017, it was steered into Saturn on purpose, so it could never crash into Enceladus and contaminate it.

visual.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

claims.text: On the 15th of September 2017, it was steered into Saturn on purpose, so it could never crash into Enceladus and contaminate it.

shots.voiceover: But the jets are still going. In 2023, the James Webb Space Telescope showed the plume reaching nearly ten thousand kilometres into space.

visual.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, G. Villanueva (NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center), A. Pagan (STScI)
visual.credit_short: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, G. Villanueva (NASA's Goddard Space F

claims.text: But the jets are still going. In 2023, the James Webb Space Telescope showed the plume reaching nearly ten thousand kilometres into space.

shots.voiceover: That is about nineteen times the width of the moon itself.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: That is about nineteen times the width of the moon itself.

shots.voiceover: In 2024, the European Space Agency named Enceladus the top target for its next large science mission.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: In 2024, the European Space Agency named Enceladus the top target for its next large science mission.

shots.voiceover: The idea: land near the tiger stripes and catch the ocean as it falls back down. The earliest launch: the 2040s.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

claims.text: The idea: land near the tiger stripes and catch the ocean as it falls back down. The earliest launch: the 2040s.

shots.voiceover: So, is something alive in the ocean of Enceladus?

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: Nobody knows. Not yet.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: But for the first time, we know a place in our solar system where every ingredient is there,

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)

shots.voiceover: and the ocean sends us samples for free. We just have to go and catch them.

visual.credit: Our visualization: Enceladus map PIA18435 (NASA/JPL/SSI/LPI), Saturn and ring textures Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0)
